signals.excerpt:
SAN MATEO, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Neo4j Ⓡ, the world’s leading graph intelligence platform, today released Relate, an AI-native, open source, in-memory and in-process embedded database built in Rust for AI Agents and Agentic Systems. With Relate, AI coding agents can create a database and start building applications in milliseconds.

...

Native Agent Integration Built-in 

 Relate, released as open source under the Apache 2.0 license, brings multihop reasoning capabilities and GraphRAG to AI agents for more accurate results and fewer hallucinations. The database is engineered specifically for the execution loops of autonomous agents. It natively auto-detects agent harnesses and returns structured errors equipped with explicit retryable flags. These flags enable agents to handle exceptions and self-correct without custom parsing logic. Relate enforces a row cap combined with an in-band truncation marker to prevent context window saturation during large retrievals. This constraint ensures agents receive bounded and predictable payloads.

...

The new embedded in-memory database for AI agents deploys seamlessly across Jupyter notebooks, web browsers, software containers, and edge devices. It runs natively wherever agents are at work. The database ships with built-in agent connectivity via a Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server and a dedicated CLI for direct execution. Relate also exposes Bolt and HTTP Query API v2 endpoints to provide drop-in support for existing graph drivers, orchestration frameworks, and standard developer tooling.

...

Relate delivers sub-millisecond reads in memory to handle the high-frequency read/write cycles of agentic workloads. A single Cypher statement can search by vector similarity and execute graph traversals simultaneously. The database maintains strict transactional integrity using an in-memory engine with an optional fsync'd write-ahead log for durable stores. It provides native options to flush state to disk for long-term persistence. Relate is 100% openCypher and more than 97% GQL compliant out of the box.

signals.title: Together AI Unveils FOSCAR to Accelerate LLM Inference on NVIDIA GPUs | Tech Pulse | TheNextGenTechInsider
signals.excerpt:
# Together AI Unveils FOSCAR to Accelerate LLM Inference on NVIDIA GPUs

Researchers have introduced FOSCAR, a kernel library that utilizes affine folding to optimize 2-bit and 4-bit KV cache decoding. The tool provides significant speedups for LLM inference on NVIDIA H100 and B200 architectures.

...

Nov 11, 2026• 3 min read

...

Researchers from Together AI and the University of Sydney have introduced FOSCAR, a kernel library designed to optimize 2-bit and 4-bit key-s-value (KV) cache decoding for large language model (LLM) inference, according to their research paper.

The development addresses a critical bottleneck in low-bit quantization: while compressing the KV cache reduces high-bandwidth memory (HBM) traffic, the instruction-issue throughput required to dequantize each element—specifically applying scale and offset—often limits latency gains. On H100 GPUs, existing fused kernels have been shown to reach less than 31% of peak HBM throughput due to this arithmetic overhead source.

...

FOSCAR utilizes a technique called affine folding to bypass per-element dequantization. Instead of applying scale and offset to every individual value, the kernel applies these transformations to the partial matrix products or the query/value operands.

Key technical specifications include:

- Mathematical Equivalence: Affine folding produces the same attention output as full dequantization while reducing scale-and-offset operations by up to two orders of magnitude source.
- Hardware Optimization: The library features warp-specialized pipelines specifically tuned for NVIDIA Hopper (H100) and Blackwell (B200) architectures, utilizing `wgmma` and `tcgen05` instructions.
- Instruction Efficiency: Optimized bit manipulation allows for direct feeding of KV operands to Tensor Cores, requiring only 1 and 0.19 ALU instructions per element for INT2 on H100 and B200, respectively source.

## Performance Results

Benchmarks demonstrate substantial speedups across modern NVIDIA architectures:

- NVIDIA H100: FOSCAR INT2 and INT4 kernels achieved geometric-mean speedups of $3.36\times$ and $2.83\times$ over the FlashInfer BF16 baseline source.
- NVIDIA B200: The kernels achieved speedups of $2.67\times$ (INT2) and $2.30\times$ (INT4) over FlashInfer BF16 source.
- Serving Throughput: When integrated into the SGLang engine, FOSCAR increased peak aggregate throughput on long-context workloads by up to $170\%$ compared to 2-bit baselines and $341\%$ compared to 16-bit baselines source.

## Availability

The FOSCAR kernel library is open-source and available via GitHub.

signals.title: Start and Restore GPU Workloads in Seconds with NVIDIA Snapshot | NVIDIA Technical Blog
signals.excerpt:
# Start and Restore GPU Workloads in Seconds with NVIDIA Snapshot

 Nov 10, 2026 

 By Ron Kahn, Dan Feigin, Oz Bar-Shalom, Ekin Karabulut and Schwinn Saereesitthipitak

...

- NVIDIA Snapshot is an open-source checkpoint and restore system for GPU workloads on Kubernetes that captures fully initialized CPU and GPU memory state.
- Restoring from a Snapshot artifact brings inference replicas online in 3.6 to 42.7 seconds across tested configurations, delivering 8x to 36x speedups over cold starts that take minutes.
- The system supports multi-GPU workloads using tensor parallelism, data and expert parallelism, and decode context parallelism for large mixture-of-experts models with checkpoints up to 1 TB across eight GPUs.
- Checkpoint creation takes 15 seconds to 5.5 minutes depending on model size, and the combined checkpoint-plus-restore time is shorter than a single cold start in every tested configuration.
- Benchmark results on NVIDIA B200 GPUs with VAST NFS storage show that restoring GPU state dominates large restores at 18 to 29 seconds, while CRIU-based CPU process restore takes 4.2 to 10.8 seconds.

...

NVIDIA Snapshot, a new open-source component of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform, makes initialized GPU workloads reusable across inference replicas—speeding startup and recovery.

When inference demand spikes or a replica fails, available GPUs don’t translate immediately into serving capacity. Initializing an LLM workload—a process known as a cold start—can take minutes, delaying scaling and recovery.

Snapshot is a checkpoint and restore system for GPU workloads on Kubernetes. It captures a fully initialized workload—including CPU and GPU memory—and restores that state on compatible infrastructure, bringing inference capacity online in seconds instead of minutes. Figure 1 shows the startup sequence. Snapshot skips repeated workload initialization; infrastructure provisioning and container image loading remain outside the measured restore path.

...

- Crusoe, an upstream contributor to Snapshot, reduced GLM-5.3 Pod readiness time from roughly 8 minutes to 31 seconds on NVIDIA HGX B300.
- Saturn Cloud, a token factory platform, benchmarked NVIDIA Snapshot for scale-from-zero inference, cutting vLLM startup from 2–8.5 minutes to 6–34 seconds on NVIDIA HGX B300.

The following benchmarks show how Snapshot accelerates inference startup across vLLM, SGLang, and NVIDIA TensorRT LLM (TRT-LLM)—with models from 600 million parameters to mixture-of-experts (MoE) models with 1 TB checkpoints on 8 GPUs. Across all tested configurations, Snapshot brings a replica back in under 45 seconds, 8x to 36x faster than a cold start.

...

### Setup

- GPU: NVIDIA B200
- NVIDIA driver: 615.71.09
- Storage backend: VAST (NFS)
- Inference engines:

- vLLM 0.31.0
- SGLang 0.5.21
- TensorRT LLM 1.3.0

### Results

The benchmarks show four main findings.

- Restore times stayed under 43 seconds: Across all tested configurations, Snapshot restored replicas in 3.6 to 42.7 seconds—8x to 36x faster than cold start. The largest MoE models, with checkpoints of about 600 GB to 1 TB across eight GPUs, restored in under 43 seconds compared with cold-start times of 6 to 19 minutes.
- Restoring skips more than weight loading: Cold-start time includes loading weights, compiling and autotuning kernels, and capturing CUDA graphs. Snapshot restores the initialized workload, skipping these repeated steps.
- Checkpointing pays off with the first restored replica: In every tested configuration, checkpoint time plus restore time was shorter than a single cold start. Checkpoint creation took 15 seconds to 5.5 minutes, depending on the model and configuration.
- Moving GPU state dominates large restores: For the eight-GPU MoE configurations, restoring GPU state took 18 to 29 seconds. Restoring CPU process state with CRIU took 4.2 to 10.8 seconds.

signals.title: RagLeap v0.13.1 and ragleap-memory 0.3.0: Better Action Auditing and Optional Vector Search - DEV Community
signals.excerpt:
# RagLeap v0.13.1 and ragleap-memory 0.3.0: Better Action Auditing and Optional Vector Search 

RagLeap has two new releases focused on an important part of building reliable AI systems: understanding what agents do and improving how they retrieve information.

- ragleap-core v0.13.1 introduces structured audit log lines for agent actions.
- ragleap-memory 0.3.0 adds optional vector and hybrid search using an embedder function supplied by the developer.

Both releases are open-source and designed for self-hosted environments.

...

## 2. ragleap-memory 0.3.0: Optional Vector and Hybrid Search 

The second release focuses on memory retrieval.

Ragleap Memory 0.3.0 adds vector and hybrid search while keeping keyword search as the default.

One design decision is particularly important: the library does not include provider-specific embedding code, API keys, or network access.

Developers supply their own embedder function.

This gives applications control over where embedding requests go and which embedding implementation they use.

### New search modes 

The library supports three search modes:

- `keyword` — the default and existing search behaviour.
- `vector` — cosine similarity over stored vectors.
- `hybrid` — combines keyword and vector results using reciprocal rank fusion.

Example: 

```
results = store.search(
    "relevant information",
    mode="hybrid",
    query_vector=query_vector,
)

```

The exact embedder and vector-generation workflow are controlled by the application.

...

### Security and limitations 

There are important limitations developers should understand:

- Stored vectors are currently unencrypted and may reveal information about the original text.
- Text sent to an embedder leaves the process wherever that embedder sends it.
- Vector search scans at most `max_vector_candidates` eligible entries.
- Retrieval quality depends on the selected embedder and has not yet been measured.
- No independent security review has been completed.

...

RagLeap is an open-source, self-hosted AI employee platform. We welcome developers, testers, technical writers, and contributors interested in building practical AI infrastructure.

signals.title: Introducing TPU Sync: Fast KV cache & weight transfer on TPU | Google Cloud Blog
signals.excerpt:
Introducing TPU Sync: Fast KV cache and weight transfer for inference and RL on TPU

November 9, 2026

...

As frontier AI evolves from stateless single-turn prompts to million-token agents, disaggregated serving, and continuous reinforcement learning (RL), the primary bottleneck in AI infrastructure has shifted from raw compute to orchestrating live model state — both the contextual state held in massive key-value (KV) caches during inference and the parameter state updated and broadcast from trainers to rollout samplers during RL. Whenever this state is trapped inside a single chip's memory or stalled on network transfers, AI accelerators sit idle.

We designed TPU Sync from first principles to serve as the model-state layer across TPU clusters — built on the architectural insight that accelerator High Bandwidth Memory (HBM), host DRAM, shared storage, and the data center network (DCN) should operate as a single, co-designed memory hierarchy. An open-source, native C++ library, TPU Sync moves TPU-tiled tensors directly across this hierarchy with asynchronous DMA transfers that overlap data movement with active computation.

For inference, it decouples TPU compute from network backpressure and turns host DRAM, local SSDs, and Google Cloud Managed Lustre into an automated, multi-tier KV cache; and for RL, it exposes low-level DMA and DCN primitives that higher-level RL frameworks can use to stream updated weights from trainers to samplers. By accessing device buffers in place rather than copying or locking them, TPU Sync consistently slashes KV transfer latency by over 90% and reduces Time to First Token (TTFT) by an average of 90% for heavyweight open-weight MoE models (235B–480B parameters) in prefix-caching and disaggregated-serving workloads, compared to running without TPU Sync.

...

- Long-context AI agents and multi-turn chats: When interacting with an AI agent over an extended 256K to 1M+ token session or analyzing massive documents, the model generates a continuously growing KV cache. Instead of allowing this state to exhaust HBM capacity, TPU Sync automatically tiers older KV blocks out of TPU HBM and into large pools of host RAM (with experimental tiering to shared secondary storage).
- Enterprise applications with heavy system prompts (prefix caching): AI serving platforms receive thousands of queries that share common instructions or documents. Rather than recomputing prefixes that the model has already processed, TPU Sync extends the prefix cache into distributed host memory so concurrent sessions can reuse precomputed KV blocks and bypass redundant prefill computation.
- Disaggregated serving architecture (prefill/decode): In modern enterprise deployments, workloads are isolated: Compute-bound nodes process the initial massive prompt (prefill), while memory-bound nodes draft the response token-by-token (decode). TPU Sync bridges this hardware gap by acting as a high-bandwidth Host-to-Host (H2H) streaming pipeline. It routes the processed context directly from the prefill nodes to the decode nodes, consistently delivering an over 90% reduction in data transfer overhead.
- Reinforcement learning pipelines (experimental): Validated on internal RL workloads and included in the repository as an experimental module, TPU Sync provides low-level DMA and DCN transfer primitives that higher-level RL frameworks can use to synchronize model weights between trainers and inference samplers — including automatic resharding across different trainer and sampler parallelism layouts — to reduce the time rollout workers spend waiting on weight updates.

...

- Over 90% KV transfer overhead cut: For heavyweight models like Qwen3 235B, median KV transfer latency dropped from several seconds down to a flat ~230 ms.
- Substantial TTFT reduction: Demonstrated an average of 60% reduction in TTFT for heavyweight models (Qwen3 235B) under controlled, low-concurrency testing benchmarks, and an average of 90% for 480B under low concurrency.
- Substantial high-traffic scalability: During sustained traffic spikes, TPU Sync achieves an average of 30% to 70% increase in token output throughput for 235B, depending on traffic distribution.

...

TPU Sync is available today as open source with Python wheels for both PyTorch (`tpu-sync-torch`) and JAX (`tpu-sync-jax`), and is integrated with vLLM-TorchTPU, SGLang-TorchTPU, and llm-d on GKE. Visit the GitHub repository to explore the architecture docs, C++ and Python APIs, and deployment guides.

signals.title: 9 open-source tools that give AI coding agents real context - DEV Community
signals.excerpt:
TL;DR: "context" means three different things for an agent: the structure of your code, the docs of other people's libraries, and plain fast search. Pick one tool per job instead of one tool for everything.

...

### 1. Graphify: a knowledge graph of your repo 

Graphify (Apache-2.0, ~145k ⭐) turns a codebase, plus its docs, SQL schemas, configs and PDFs, into a queryable knowledge graph. Parsing is local and deterministic (AST, no embeddings, no vector store), and every edge is tagged `EXTRACTED` (read straight from the source) or `INFERRED` (resolved by Graphify), so you can see why two things are connected. 

```
pip install graphifyy
graphify path "FastAPI" "ModelField"
graphify explain "APIRouter"

```

You get a `graph.json`, an interactive `graph.html`, and a `GRAPH_REPORT.md` with the most-connected "god nodes" and Leiden communities (your subsystems). It runs as a `/graphify` skill in Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and Gemini CLI, and there's an MCP server via `graphifyy[mcp]`. If you'd rather not run anything locally, the hosted version is at app.graphify.com.

Use it when the question is "how does X connect to Y?" or "what breaks if I touch this?"

...

Serena ... It does this by driving real language servers (LSP), and the README lists support for over 40 languages.

...

### 7. Claude Context: semantic search over your code 

Claude Context (MIT, ~13k ⭐) from Zilliz is an MCP server that indexes your codebase into a vector database (Milvus or Zilliz Cloud) so the agent can search by meaning. It's the most "classic RAG" pick here, and it needs a vector DB and an embedding provider to run.

Use it when your questions are fuzzy ("where do we handle retries?") and you're fine running a vector store.

...

GitMCP: any GitHub repo as an MCP server 

GitMCP (Apache-2.0, ~8.5k ⭐) is a free, remote MCP server. Point your agent at `https://gitmcp.io/{owner}/{repo}` and it can read that project's docs and code, even if the model has never seen it. There's also a generic `gitmcp.io/docs` endpoint for switching between repos.

...

## How I'd combine them 

- One structure tool for your own repo: Graphify for relationships across code and docs, or Serena for symbol-level navigation.
- One search tool: ast-grep for exact syntax, Probe for ranked results, Claude Context if you want semantic search.
- One docs tool: Context7 for popular libraries, GitMCP for everything else.

signals.title: PyTorch introduces ExecuTorch WebGPU for browser GPU inference
signals.excerpt:
# PyTorch introduces ExecuTorch WebGPU backend to run models on the GPU in the browser

PyTorch introduced the ExecuTorch WebGPU backend, letting models run on the GPU in WebGPU browsers through a single .pte export. It keeps inference local, so user data does not leave the device.

...

PyTorch has introduced a WebGPU backend for ExecuTorch that lets PyTorch models run on the GPU inside a web browser without converting to another framework's format. Developers export a model with `torch.export` to a `.pte` file, and PyTorch says the same artifact runs in any WebGPU browser through ExecuTorch's WebAssembly runtime.

The backend covers a broad range of model families: large language models such as Llama 3.2, Qwen3, and Gemma 3; vision-language models including SmolVLM; vision tasks like Depth Anything V2, SAM 2, D-FINE, Real-ESRGAN, and background removal; and speech models such as Whisper and Phonon. On-device LoRA and DiReFT fine-tuning for Llama 3.2 1B, Qwen2.5 0.5B, and Qwen3 0.6B is also supported. PyTorch says inference stays in the browser tab, with no data leaving the device.

On an Apple M1 Pro running Chrome, the WebGPU backend is 4–7× faster than ExecuTorch's WebAssembly CPU path (XNNPACK, multi-threaded) on prefill and 2–10× faster on decode, according to PyTorch's own benchmarks using quantized Llama 3.2 1B and Qwen3-0.6B. The WebGPU implementation relies on 4-bit groupwise weights (group size 64) alongside fp32 activations, whereas XNNPACK powers the CPU baseline with 4-bit weights and 8-bit dynamic activations. Each data point is the median of five runs after three warmups across 128 to 8K tokens of context.

The design rests on three principles: a single export through torch.export() and the WebGPUPartitioner, which runs via WGSL compute shaders; one .pte artifact usable across browsers and native platforms (Metal on macOS, Vulkan on Linux and Android, D3D12 on Windows) by translating WGSL to the platform shading language; and frictionless deployment, because a .pte file served over a CDN executes in a browser sandbox without requiring a native installation, backend server, or any data to leave the device. Pipeline compilation, memory management, and dispatch scheduling are handled by the WebGPU backend, with all data remaining in GPU device memory within the tab.

PyTorch provides an ExecuTorch WebGPU Playground where many of the validated models can be tried directly. Each model's Hugging Face repository holds the .pte files, a model card and the export recipe. A linked Hugging Face repository says the converted Llama 3.2 1B Instruct model has a total size of 709.5 MB, applies q4gsw (group size 64) to every linear layer and the tied token embedding/output head, retains activations and KV cache in fp32, and limits context to 8,960 tokens (upstream is 128K), while processing at most 512 tokens per forward call. The same card says the WebAssembly runtime build behind these files is not published yet, so for now they are meant to be run through the playground. It also warns that 4-bit quantization changes the outputs: on three test prompts, greedy text agreed with the fp32 model for 6 tokens, 8 tokens (the whole answer) and 0 tokens, though all three answers stayed fluent and on topic.

PyTorch calls the backend early development, and the ExecuTorch README still lists both the browser runtime and WebGPU as experimental. PyTorch says it will continue improving speed and stability while expanding operator, data type, and model coverage. The project is open source under a BSD license, and contributions — new operators, models, or performance improvements — are welcomed via GitHub issues or the ExecuTorch Discord.

...

- PyTorch tests, Apple M1 Pro in Chrome: 4–7× faster on prefill, 2–10× on decode against ExecuTorch's Wasm CPU path (XNNPACK)
- Llama 3.2 1B conversion: 709.5 MB, 8,960-token context cap, at most 512 tokens per forward call

...

- No independent replication of the 4–7× / 2–10× speedup claims on other hardware or browsers.
- GA / stable release date for the WebGPU backend not stated; labeled early development.
- Full operator coverage matrix and data-type support list not published.
- Memory footprint and thermal behavior on mobile devices (phones, tablets) not disclosed.
- When the WebGPU WebAssembly runtime build will be published.

signals.title: Railtown AI Ships Open-Source Swift RAG for On-Device Agents | The Cloud Nation
signals.excerpt:
Railtown AI Technologies Inc. released Railtracks Swift RAG on Nov. 9, an open-source library that lets Apple developers turn PDFs, text, CSV and JSON files into searchable Knowledge Bases stored on the user's device, according to Yahoo! Finance.

The library sits inside the company's Railtracks Swift Agent Development Kit, published Oct. 21, and is distributed under an MIT license from the Railtracks Swift repository. No commercial license from Railtown is required.

...

Railtracks Swift RAG ingests documents and splits them into searchable passages. A retrieval-augmented generation pipeline then hands those passages to a language model, which answers the user's question from the user's own files rather than from general training data.

Retrieved passages keep references to their source documents. An application can therefore show which passage supports a generated answer.

When configured with Apple's supported on-device embeddings and language models, ingestion, retrieval and response generation all run locally. Documents, questions and retrieved passages do not need to reach a remote AI provider.

Cloud embeddings remain available. Developers choose local, cloud or hybrid configurations and take responsibility for external services, connected tools and application logging.

...

AI Travel Planner coordinates six specialized agents. The agents pull travel data from external services, assemble an itinerary and store the result in a local knowledge base that users can query by voice.

...

The local-processing guarantee covers the application's configured Knowledge Base and AI workflow. It does not cover every Siri interaction.

Siri requests may be processed through Apple services, and Railtown states this explicitly. The company also notes that capability availability depends on the developer's implementation, the device and the operating system version.

signals.title: Cloud Pathways, a distributed ML runtime, is GA | Google Cloud Blog
signals.excerpt:
Cloud Pathways, a distributed ML runtime for massive accelerator fleets, now GA

November 9, 2026

##### Shaurya Gupta

Software Engineer, Google

##### Monica Song

Product Manager, Google

Today, we are thrilled to announce the general availability (GA) of Cloud Pathways (Pathways on Cloud) on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) as a core runtime pillar of the Google Cloud AI Hypercomputer.

Originally engineered by Google DeepMind to train and serve Google's frontier models — including Gemini — Pathways is our distributed machine-learning runtime designed for massive, heterogeneous accelerator fleets. In fact, over the last 90 days alone, leading AI companies and global enterprises have processed more than 130 million Cloud TPU chip-hours using Pathways on GKE, across a broad range of TPU generations.

With Cloud Pathways, every Google Cloud customer can use the same single-controller runtime, colocated Python sidecars, and elastic fault tolerance that power Google's largest AI workloads. We are also pleased to announce a Preview integration with Cluster Director to extend Cloud Pathways to Slurm clusters, supporting unified multi-slice JAX execution, elastic training, and interactive notebooks.

...

Cloud Pathways has the following features:

- Single-controller orchestration: In Cloud Pathways, a single controller manages graph evaluation, persistent Cloud Storage compilation caching, and asynchronous XLA HLO dispatch across TPU slices.
- Colocated Python sidecars: Client-side colocated Python sidecar containers (with shared-memory support) let you run compute-intensive Python logic such as distributed data loading and checkpointing directly on TPU hosts.
- Resilient and elastic training: Cloud Pathways decouples job survival from individual slice interruptions with elastic training (`pathwaysutils`) using host-memory snapshots to dynamically reshard training down to N-1 slices during hardware failures without crashing the client.
- Interactive mode and Shared Pathways Service: Run, inspect, and debug JAX workloads interactively from a notebook or terminal using interactive mode, or share a long-running pool of Cloud TPU slices on demand across multiple users and jobs with the Shared Pathways Service.

...

Cloud Pathways is generally available today in all Google Cloud regions supporting Cloud TPU v5e, TPU v5p, Trillium (TPU v6e), and Ironwood (TPU 7x) on GKE, with versioned container images (`us-docker.pkg.dev/cloud-tpu-v2-images/cloud-pathways`) supporting JAX `0.10.1+`. Cloud Pathways is also available in Preview on Slurm TPU clusters in Cluster Director.

signals.title: Scaling AI agents with open standards: Kurtis Van Gent on MCP and Agent Skills joining the AAIF | Google Open Source Blog
signals.excerpt:
Over the past year, open source communities have rallied around two complementary open standards to solve these challenges: the Model Context Protocol (MCP) for connecting agents to live tools, and Agent Skills for loading procedural instructions and scripts on demand. Following Anthropic's donation of the Agent Skills specification to the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) alongside MCP, engineers from Google, Anthropic, OpenAI, and the wider ecosystem are now co-maintaining the standard under vendor-neutral governance.

...

At the time, most database conversations focused on retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) using vector search. However, our team believed that agents and tools held the most interesting potential for large language models (LLMs) going forward. We immediately hit two scaling challenges: Google Cloud supports more than 15 different databases across its portfolio, and new open source agent frameworks (starting with LangChain and LlamaIndex) were emerging every week.

That created a classic N-by-M integration problem between many clients and many data hosts. To solve it, we started GenAI Toolbox for Databases (now MCP Toolbox for Databases) as an open source framework for building and serving tools. We built our own server, clients, and protocol to standardize how agents look up and invoke database tools. Back then, agent terminology wasn't common vernacular yet, so every talk I gave had to start with three to five slides explaining what agents and tools actually were.

...

Agent Skills introduced a remarkably simple, effective pattern for solving that problem through progressive disclosure. By loading only a lightweight YAML frontmatter name and description at startup, and pulling the full `SKILL.md` instructions, reference files, or scripts into context only when a task requires them, Agent Skills commoditized context the same way MCP commoditized tools.

...

At the platform level, our Google Cloud Databases team pairs MCP and Agent Skills together inside our Agent Plugins. When a developer using Antigravity connects to a PostgreSQL database on Cloud SQL or AlloyDB, they can install the corresponding Cloud SQL or AlloyDB plugin. From MCP, the agent gets a list of safe actions it can take against the database. From the bundled Agent Skills, it gets step-by-step instructions on how to use those tools for specific tasks, like provisioning an instance or configuring Identity and Access Management (IAM) database authentication securely—and because both specifications are open standards, the same `SKILL.md` and MCP pattern works across any open source database or agent harness.

signals.title: Meituan Open-Sources LongCat-2.5: Long-Sequence SFT Single-GPU Throughput Up 86% vs. DDP
signals.excerpt:
# Meituan Open-Sources LongCat-2.5: Long-Sequence SFT Single-GPU Throughput Up 86% vs. DDP

Time : Nov 10, 2026 Read : 4 minute

Meituan open-sourced LongCat-2.5 on November 10 under the MIT License. It supports commercial inference deployment and further training without additional authorization. The model targets long-horizon agent tasks and features a native multimodal architecture, with 1.6 trillion total parameters, about 48 billion parameters activated per token, and support for a one-million-token context. It significantly improves end-to-end delivery capabilities in complex codebase development, complete project construction, Visual Coding, and professional office scenarios. The weights are available on HuggingFace, with the technical blog and API platform also opened simultaneously.

...

It performs residual vector quantization on native-resolution features, progressively filling in details level by level. ... On the professional office side, it strengthens material processing and professional judgment, enabling end-to-end delivery of reports, presentations, and office tools.

Inference adopts the W4A4 scheme, quantizing expert weights and activations to 4-bit and executing them on native INT4 matrix multiplication units. FlatQuant is used to optimize MoE quantization accuracy, with downstream performance comparable to that before quantization, while dedicated fused operators help reduce costs. Both training and supervised fine-tuning use long-sequence training. Targeting domestic AI accelerators with less than 80GB of VRAM per card, it uses FSDP double sharding and hybrid vocabulary parallelism to distribute memory pressure. This configuration increases per-GPU throughput in long-sequence SFT by 86% over the DDP baseline, providing an efficiency foundation for open-source deployment of trillion-parameter MoE models.

What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models
            
            
            - Google Developers Blog
signals.excerpt:
## TLDR

Today, we announce the General Availability of Pathways on Google Cloud Platform. In this post, you will learn about Pathways, the distributed system Google built to train its own large models, including Gemini. We discuss how Pathways addresses the coordination challenge by introducing one client that describes the whole computation as a graph, and how the distributed runtime places it, moves the tensors, and keeps the accelerators busy.

...

That is the idea behind Pathways, the distributed system Google built to train its own largest models, including Gemini. Pathways runs JAX programs on TPUs and it is available on Google Cloud.

...

With Pathways, you define the end-to-end computation from a single Python client, without writing custom coordination code, and a distributed runtime executes it. That client is decoupled from the hardware. It runs on an ordinary CPU machine and you write your program against virtual devices; a resource manager maps them onto real chips, and a worker on each accelerator host runs the compiled programs it receives.

signals.title: RadixArk team describes serving Meta’s Muse Spark Open on one TPU host | AI.info
signals.excerpt:
The RadixArk team describes running Meta’s 816-billion-parameter Muse Spark Open on a single TPU v7 host using SGLang-TorchTPU. Its post details a megakernel, attention and expert-processing changes, and results on the AgentX benchmark.

...

A post by Haolin Fu, Xiaoyu Zhang, Junyan Xu, Wangyuan Zhang, Haoguang Cai and the RadixArk Team describes serving Meta’s Muse Spark Open, an 816-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model, on one TPU v7 host with four chips. The authors write, “We serve Meta’s Muse Spark Open, an 816B-parameter mixture-of-experts model, on a single TPU v7 host of four chips, with SGLang running on the TorchTPU PyTorch backend.” Their post describes SGLang-TorchTPU with Pallas kernels handling performance-critical work.

...

The central change is a megakernel: one Pallas program on each device handles all 62 layers of a decode or verification step. SGLang continues to run the embedding, draft model, KV-cache write, language-model head and sampling around that program, the post says.

For a single request, the megakernel takes 1.95 milliseconds per output token, compared with 3.78 milliseconds on the native path, a 1.94-times speedup. Figure 4 measures the verify-step comparison with DFlash2 speculative decoding on GSM8K using an earlier Muse Spark checkpoint. The RadixArk team reports a 1.85-times speedup for two concurrent requests; the gain narrows as concurrency increases.

...

In the serving system, the pipelined attention loop ... A separate kernel test with random routing showed decode steps with many requests running 13% to 19% faster after the team split its expert-processing work into two loops.

...

For the 1-million-context version of SemiAnalysis’s AgentX coding benchmark, the post reports a range from 433 output tokens per second per request at 6,101 tokens per second per chip, to 25,906 tokens per second per chip at 95 tokens per second per request. Every TPU result shown finished requests within 47 seconds at the 90th percentile.

Announcement · November 11, 2026

# Pipeline Parallelism is here: 8x faster than Apple’s WWDC26 fine-tuning

One 48 GB MacBook Pro ran Apple’s WWDC26 fine-tuning faster than Apple’s four M3 Ultra Mac Studios. Four MacBook Pros ran it more than 8× faster.

We are a small team, twelve months, our own mathematics, and a Tensor Engine built from the ground up. This is what it does.

1,440.8 tokens/s · NukeTorch, one MacBook Pro M5 Max

tokens/s · Apple’s WWDC26 run, four M3 Ultra (Apple’s figure)

5,358.5 tokens/s · NukeTorch, four MacBook Pro M5 Max

8×+ faster than Apple’s WWDC26 run, every run

Today we also release NukeTorch for one Mac as a free download, so you can test our speed yourself.

...

At WWDC 2026, Apple fine-tuned Qwen3.5-9B with MLX: about 180 tokens/s on one M3 Ultra Mac Studio, and about 600 on four. We ran Apple’s recipe, with Apple’s own commands, on MacBook Pros.

| | Apple, WWDC26 | NukeTorch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One machine | ~180 tokens/s One M3 Ultra Mac Studio | 1,440.8 tokens/s One MacBook Pro M5 Max, 48 GB |
| Four machines | ~600 tokens/s Four M3 Ultra Mac Studios | 5,358.5 tokens/s Four MacBook Pro M5 Max, 48 GB each |
| Method on four machines | Data parallel | Pipeline parallel |
| 1,000 steps on four machines | About 40½ minutes at that speed | Under 5 minutes |

The machines differ, and Apple’s figures are the ones spoken in its session. We did not run Apple’s setup. One machine trains 4 examples per step and four machines train 16, as in Apple’s two commands. Every four-Mac run of ours was more than 8× Apple’s figure. The slowest was 8.45×.

...

Pipeline parallelism does not make a single prompt faster. Our speed comes from the mathematics. NukeTorch spreads one model across many machines without the usual inefficiency and without special interconnects. Each machine holds its assigned layers of the model, and together they work as one distributed machine.

- It keeps the speed.

...

- It needs a fraction of the memory. Qwen3.8 Flash Next is 106.3 GB. Pi

...

- It uses less energy.

...

No single 48 GB Mac can hold it. The pipeline splits it across four Macs, nothing is stored twice, and all four serve every user together.

...

Qwen3.6 35B-A3B, Qwen3.8 27B and NVIDIA’s GR00T N1.7 each fit in one Mac. Here each of the four MacBook Pros runs its own server and serves its own users.

| Model | One user per Mac | 32 users at once, 8 per Mac |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Qwen3.6 35B-A3B, 4-bit | 510.9 tokens/s per user | 3,799.6 tokens/s combined |
| Qwen3.8 27B, 4-bit | 203.2 tokens/s per user | 1,906.2 tokens/s combined |

...

signals.title: JioHotstar Benchmarks Knowledge Bases for AI Coding Agents - InfoQ
signals.excerpt:
JioHotstar evaluated six approaches to helping AI coding agents navigate large codebases, finding that structural code search performed well on clearly defined engineering tasks, while semantic retrieval helped more with ambiguous requirements. The evaluation also found that adding retrieval layers did not consistently improve task completion or reduce token consumption.

Abhishek Bansal, Senior Staff Engineer at JioHotStar, compared filesystem tools, Sourcebot, Graphify, CocoIndex Code, Repowise, and an in-house retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline. The team evaluated the approaches using subsets of SWE-bench and CodeScaleBench, alongside a custom question-answering harness for JioHotstar's codebase. The experiments used Claude Sonnet as the solving model and measured task accuracy, token consumption, agent turns, and tool usability.

...

The filesystem baseline, which relied on locally checked out repositories and standard search and file operations, remained competitive on concrete tasks. Sourcebot, which provides indexed text search, symbol definitions, references, and file reads, performed better than the baseline on harder SWE-bench Verified tasks while also costing less. On simpler SWE-bench Lite tasks, retrieval generally added overhead without consistently improving results.

CodeScaleBench showed a different pattern. Semantic retrieval helped more when agents had to interpret ambiguous problem descriptions and map them to implementation details that were not obvious from exact text or symbol searches. The findings suggest that retrieval approaches should be selected according to task characteristics rather than treated as interchangeable solutions.

...

JioHotstar's evaluation did not identify a single retrieval approach that performed best across all tasks. Instead, JioHotstar recommends retaining filesystem tools as a baseline, using structural search for concrete, code-focused problems and semantic indexing for ambiguous or cross-cutting requirements. JioHotStar engineering team also emphasizes measuring tool-use traces alongside task accuracy to determine whether retrieval reduces unnecessary exploration. The findings highlight the importance of matching retrieval capabilities to the programming task and how the agent navigates the codebase.

signals.title: Changing how we measure AI chip inference performance | Epoch AI
signals.excerpt:
# Inference Performance Index: changing the way we measure inference capacity

Comparing AI hardware for inference beyond FLOP/s with memory and inter-chip communication

...

Inference performance improvements can be much larger than changes in raw compute speed (FLOP/s) suggest. We estimate that the Nvidia GB300 provides about 25× Nvidia H100’s inference capacity per chip on the agentic inference workloads we model, with only 2.5× the 8-bit FLOP per second.

Comparing FLOP/s alone would therefore underestimate GB300’s inference capacity relative to H100 by a factor of ten. This is because memory and inter-chip communication can matter more than arithmetic throughput for inference performance.

We introduce the Inference Performance Index (IPI) to capture these differences. The index compares how many requests each chip can serve at once across a range of required output speeds. IPI Version 1 focuses on agentic workloads and combines results across four representative models.

...

Within Blackwell Ultra, GB300 NVL72 scores about 1.9× B300 HGX (0.54), highlighting the importance of its larger scale-up domain. MI355X scores about 0.55, while VR200 scores 2.18.

# BotPsy 0.8B On‑Device Assistant Beats Larger Models in Tool Use 

 Tether AI Research releases an open‑source, sub‑billion‑parameter model optimized for on‑device function calling. 

 By A Adel Khoury | Nov 11, 2026 · 09:18 | 2 min read AI-Synthesized Report 

 GazeWire — Source: Hugging Face Blog 

## 30-second key takeaways 

- BotPsy is a 0.8 B‑parameter on‑device assistant that outperforms models up to 2.5× larger on six tool‑use benchmarks.
- Agentic performance metrics (BFCL v4, ACEBench, τ‑bench) more than double compared with its base model.
- Safety testing shows the lowest unsafe response rate (21 %) among models ≤1.2 B parameters.
- The model is open‑source, available in multiple precisions, and designed for privacy‑preserving deployment on edge devices.

...

BotPsy, a 0.8 billion‑parameter model built on Qwen3.5‑0.8B, targets function‑calling and agentic workflows that can run locally on smartphones, tablets, or edge gateways. It is positioned as a personal assistant for tasks such as web research, travel planning, finance queries, device control, calendar management and messaging, and is intended for low‑ to medium‑difficulty use cases. 

## Benchmark Performance # 

- BFCL v4 score rises from 23.4 to 44.0, more than double the base model.
- ACEBench improves from 30.1 to 58.7, setting the best result among models ≤1.2B parameters.
- τ‑bench jumps from 23.2 to 51.5, surpassing the 2.5× larger Qwen3.5‑2B‑Think on five of six tests.
- ToolSandbox climbs from 30.5 to 64.6, outpacing all competitors in the sub‑1.2B class.
- Safety‑related hallucination score reaches 86.1, the highest across the evaluated set.
- Instruction‑following accuracy (IFEval) increases from 59.7 to 90.8.

 Across the same benchmarks, BotPsy also reduces the number of reasoning tokens required for correct answers by up to threefold, which translates into lower latency on limited hardware. The model’s unsafe response rate under automated red‑team testing falls to 21 %, the lowest among peers.

...

BotPsy will be released under the Apache 2.0 license with weights in safetensors and GGUF formats (bf16, Q8, Q4), enabling integration via the QVAC SDK or llama.cpp. Future work aims to expand peer‑to‑peer encrypted web search, fine‑tune locally on user preferences, and allow secure hand‑off of heavy workloads to trusted home PCs or edge nodes.

signals.title: Agent memory is eating GraphRAG's lunch, and rerankers just got a lot cheaper
signals.excerpt:
This digest covers RAG and GraphRAG developments from 2026-10-19 through 2026-11-09: new retrieval and reranking papers from arXiv and Hugging Face Daily Papers, agent-memory architecture writeups from Anthropic and LangChain, document-parsing and graph-tooling updates from LlamaIndex and Neo4j, and a production deep-dive from Latent Space.

## 🔥 Highlights 

1. The components of agent memory — Anthropic's own layered memory architecture, with data on when curation beats raw search. 
2. Building Evidence-Grounded Agent Memory with OpenWiki and Graphs — a graph layer beats a wiki alone, without full GraphRAG overhead.
3. Agentic GraphRAG and an explorer for your own stack — a runnable reference agent over a real knowledge graph, published today. 
4. Re³Rank: Listwise Reranking with Reasoning-Conditioned Retrieval Heads — a 0.6B reranker beating 32B models, straight cost win.
5. RAGCompass: Generalizable Retriever Routing via Reranking — a trainable router for picking the right retriever per query.

...

- ArcRAG: Agentic Compositional Retrieval over Knowledge Graphs — 2026-11-04. Builds a query-specific view of a knowledge graph at inference time from the entities named in the question, then plans and repairs multi-hop traversals as Cypher queries. Practical value: a construction-agnostic retriever that works whether your graph came from a schema-guided or an open-extraction pipeline.
- Typed-Centrality Grounding for Agentic GraphRAG: A Symbolic Approach for Agentic Reasoning — 2026-11-06. Computes centrality measures per entity type as a deterministic symbolic signal alongside text-similarity retrieval, targeting GraphRAG's habit of treating the graph as homogeneous. Reports more context-consistent answers on a real-world dataset — useful if your GraphRAG hallucinates relationships that pure text similarity misses.
- QueryFlow: Multi-Hop Graph Retrieval with Adaptive Query Evolution — 2026-11-03. Updates the query representation during multi-hop traversal by folding query-conditioned graph summaries back into a shared query state. Reports double-digit gains on macro Recall@10 and LLM-Acc across four multi-hop QA datasets, addressing evidence that only becomes relevant after intermediate hops.
- RAGCompass: Generalizable Retriever Routing via Reranking — 2026-11-03. Scores retrieved passages themselves to pick the best retriever per query, trained contrastively against the answers each passage set produces. Reports a 28% relative F1 gain over the best single retriever, holding up on unseen corpora/retrievers — a generalizable routing layer for teams running multiple indexes.
- Re³Rank: Listwise Reranking with Reasoning-Conditioned Retrieval Heads — 2026-11-02. A listwise reranker where a generator writes a reasoning trace first, then a scorer uses that trace to produce relevance scores. Beats 11 baselines across 9 benchmarks, with a 0.6B variant outperforming 32B rerankers — a serious latency/cost lever for production rerank stages.
- DecisionRank: On-Policy Distillation for Decision-Model Rerankers — 2026-10-30. Distills a generative reranker's ranking knowledge into a non-autoregressive "decision model" via on-policy, item-space distillation. The 8B version matches its generative counterpart while running 16-25x faster.
- Retrieving from Your Own Mistakes: On-Policy Training of Embedding Models for Multi-Hop Retrieval-Augmented Generation — 2026-10-29. Trains multi-hop retrievers on their own retrieval trajectories, including mistakes, labeling each visited state with the earliest missing gold passage. Improves evidence completeness on harder, out-of-distribution long-chain variants of HotpotQA and 2WikiMultiHopQA.
- Reliability Stress Testing of RAG Retrieval under Query-Relevant Corpus Poisoning — 2026-11-03. Stress-tests the retrieval admission step against poisoned documents, showing query-tailored poison can fully compromise a dense retriever like BGE-small. Also evaluates overlap-based admission and MMR as mitigations — a concrete checklist for RAG exposed to untrusted corpora.
- MEMOIR: A Training-Free Memory Lifecycle for Long-Horizon LLM Agents — 2026-11-05. Combines judge-gated consolidation with retrospective attribution that credits memories that actually supported past answers, plus an exploration bonus for under-used memories. Targets two real production pains directly — consolidation discarding needed evidence, and retrieval favoring stale memories — with no added LLM calls on the write path.
- Same Simulation, Different Evidence: Where Retrieved Tool Output Costs LLM Agents Accuracy — 2026-10-19. Shows that when long tool outputs are saved to files and retrieved on demand, GPT-5.1/5.2 lose 7.9-11.3 accuracy points via "evidence substitution" (answering from prior output instead of the retrieved file), while Claude models show no detectable cost. Explicitly flagging the authoritative output recovers most of the gap — a model-specific warning for agentic retrieval over tool/file outputs.
- Signed but Steerable: Measuring and Closing the Text-Vector Integrity Gap in Offline Retrieval-Augmented Generation — 2026-11-04. Shows that signed, precomputed embedding packs for offline/edge RAG only prove publisher identity, not that vectors match the text — cosine-tolerance checks and compressed-FAISS audits both fail to catch tampering. Proposes verifying quantization codes with a calibrated guard band, which caught attackers in testing — important if you ship or consume precomputed vector indexes.

signals.title: Google open sources XSE, a C++ serving engine for XLA models | LDS
signals.excerpt:
Google has open sourced XSE, the XLA Serving Engine, a C++ runtime that serves machine learning models without a Python interpreter, announced on its Open Source Blog on November 5, 2026. Google says XSE already handles more than 6 million queries per second across services including YouTube Shorts, Google Ads and Search. In its own tests on short requests, it delivered 2 to 5 times the throughput of its best Python server, using a quarter of the memory.

...

Google describes a "Train in Python, Serve in C++" workflow. Engineers write models in a framework such as JAX or PyTorch, then export them to an "XLA SavedModel" that holds the StableHLO representation of the model's function. The XLA Serving Runtime loads and runs that file, and XLA compiles the computations into native code for the target hardware.

...

The performance figures come from Google's own tests against its own baseline, so results on other models and request mixes may differ. XSE is not the only way to drop Python from serving. The Register points to PyTorch's native C++ runtime, LibTorch, and to ONNX Runtime, which supports an open graph format with Python bindings.
